The retrieved documents present directly conflicting research outcomes. d1 concludes night-shift work did not increase cancer risk in its meta-analysis [d1]. Conversely, d2 and d3 state that organizations like the IARC classify night shift work as a probable carcinogen and present research suggesting increased risk [d2, d3]. d4 also notes studies linking long-term night work to higher colorectal cancer risk [d4]. Research on whether shift work increases cancer risk yields conflicting outcomes. One large meta-analysis found "no increased risk for cancer" associated with night-shift work [d1]. However, other sources report that the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies shift work disrupting circadian rhythms as "probably carcinogenic," particularly noting associations with breast cancer [d2, d3]. Additional studies suggest long-term rotating night shift work may elevate risks for colorectal cancer [d4]. The scientific literature contains this divergence, with differences potentially arising from study designs, definitions of shift work, and populations examined [d2].
